beginner: Cayenne likes rich, well-drained soil that warms up nicely in the sun, because peppers are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a raised bed or a sheet of black plastic mulch warms it up and helps peppers get going. The most important thing is drainage: soggy soil stalls the plant, causes root and fruit rots, and the uneven watering that comes with it leads to blossom-end rot on the pods.
seasoned: Cayenne wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam that warms early in spring, since like all peppers it is a warm-season crop that sulks in cold, wet ground. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting to feed a long season and improve moisture holding. On heavy or slow-warming soil, a raised bed or a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch lifts the soil temperature and gives transplants the warm start they need. Above all the soil must drain freely: saturated ground stalls the roots, invites the Phytophthora blight and root rots peppers are prone to, and the uneven moisture it causes drives blossom-end rot on the developing pods. Steady moisture in freely draining soil is the target.

beginner: Cayenne likes soil that is slightly acidic, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Cayenne grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, the range where the nutrients peppers need stay most available; Penn State reports best yields in the 6.0 to 6.8 band, and Clemson and UGA center a slightly tighter 6.0 to 6.5. It tolerates a little either side of this, but as the soil turns strongly acidic or above about 7.0 the uptake of several nutrients tightens and growth suffers. Most Eastern and Midwestern garden soils sit naturally near the target; alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in before planting. A simple soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.

beginner: Cayenne does not need heavy feeding, and the timing matters more than the amount. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10, or a few inches of compost, into the soil before you plant. Then feed lightly with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set. The big rule: go easy on nitrogen. Too much gives you a large, leafy plant with lots of leaves but hardly any peppers. Steady watering matters more than extra fertilizer for a good crop.
seasoned: Cayenne is a moderate feeder rather than a heavy one, and the timing matters more than the amount. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet, or a few inches of compost, into the bed before transplanting. Then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods have set. The cardinal rule is to go easy on nitrogen: too much gives a big, bushy, leafy plant with plenty of foliage but few blooms and little fruit, the single most common pepper-feeding mistake. Pair modest feeding with steady moisture, since even watering, not extra fertilizer, is what fills clean pods and heads off blossom-end rot.

beginner: Your cayenne is setting its first peppers. Give it a light nitrogen feed to keep it going, but do not overdo it or you will get all leaves.
seasoned: Your cayenne has set its first pods, a good time for a light nitrogen side-dress to keep it producing. Go easy: too much nitrogen gives leaves, not peppers.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a light nitrogen feed once pods set. Do not overdo the nitrogen, or you get all leaves and few peppers.
seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress (for example calcium nitrate, 15.5-0-0) 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives foliage at the expense of pods.

beginner: Mix 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet, or a few inches of compost, into the soil before planting. Then, 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once pods set, scratch a little nitrogen fertilizer into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in. If the plant is big and leafy but not fruiting, hold off on more nitrogen.
seasoned: A common rate is 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting, then a light side-dress of about 0.5 pound of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 100 square feet 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in. Skip further nitrogen if the plants are lush and leafy but not fruiting.

beginner: Most cayenne companions are more tradition than proven science, but the sensible ones share the warm, sunny, well-watered conditions peppers like and help with pests. Basil, and a ring of nasturtiums or marigolds, can lure aphids and flea beetles away, onions and chives are traditional pest deterrents, and low crops like carrots and lettuce fit around peppers without competing. The one rule that really matters is to keep cayenne away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are close relatives that share the same pests and soil diseases.
seasoned: Most cayenne companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The useful ones share the warm, sunny, evenly watered culture peppers want and help deflect their pests: basil and a border of nasturtium or marigold are the classic aphid and flea-beetle deflectors, alliums such as onions and chives are traditional pungent deterrents, and low root or leaf crops like carrots and lettuce use different space without sharing pepper problems. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep cayenne away from its Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share its aphid-vectored viruses, flea beetle, bacterial spot, and the soilborne Phytophthora and verticillium.

beginner: Basil is a classic partner for peppers, thought to keep aphids and other pests away, and it likes the same warm, sunny, well-watered spot. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
seasoned: A traditional pepper companion said to repel aphids and thrips, and a good match because it wants the same warm, sunny, evenly watered conditions cayenne does. The pest effect is folklore rather than trial-isolated, but the shared culture makes it a natural, low-risk neighbor.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near peppers to lure aphids and flea beetles away from them. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Often planted around peppers as a trap and deterrent for aphids and flea beetles, drawing them off the crop. Trap cropping is a documented principle, though the specific nasturtium-pepper effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Onions, garlic, and chives are traditionally planted near peppers to help keep pests away, and they take up little space. A good, low-risk companion.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional pungent interplant said to deter aphids and other soft-bodied pests. The repellent effect is folk tradition rather than trial-isolated, but they use little room and do not compete heavily with peppers.

beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for peppers, grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but a cheerful, low-risk choice.
seasoned: A long-standing companion flower; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented root-knot-nematode suppression, though the interplanted marigold-pepper pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

beginner: Keep cayenne away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same pests, viruses, and soil diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share cayenne's pest and disease complex: aphids and the mosaic and other viruses they vector, the flea beetle, bacterial leaf spot, and the soilborne Phytophthora blight and verticillium wilt. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 to 4 year cycle.

beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong Tier-1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl, mottle, and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. Worse, aphids spread plant viruses, so they are a bigger threat than their feeding alone suggests.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, discoloring and mottling the foliage, curling and puckering leaves, and coating them in sticky honeydew on which sooty mold grows. Their most serious harm is indirect: aphids transmit the mosaic and other viruses that mottle, distort, and stunt pepper plants, so an aphid problem is also a virus risk.

beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. As they move around they spread viruses, so keeping their numbers down protects against disease too.
seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather and build up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. As they probe plant to plant they carry mosaic viruses into the crop, which is why aphid control and virus control go together on peppers.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them. Pull out any plant that is clearly stunted and mottled by virus, since it will not recover.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control, and remove badly virus-infected plants, which cannot be cured.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves often, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything. Keeping aphids down early is the best way to avoid the viruses they spread.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips regularly, use reflective mulch to deter aphids from young plants, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Controlling aphids early is the main defense against the viruses they carry.

beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest and can stunt or kill seedlings, while big plants shrug it off. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
seasoned: Tiny beetles chew small, round, shot-hole pits and holes through the leaves, and large numbers of these punctures can stunt or kill seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area is quickly overwhelmed. Established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.

beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and hit young plants hardest, so they are mainly a seedling problem.
seasoned: Several flea beetle species that overwinter as adults in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Large populations concentrate on small transplants, so the damage is an early-season, seedling-stage problem more than a threat to mature peppers.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants rather than tiny seedlings so plants outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.

beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium or other trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.

beginner: A fly lays eggs in young pods, and the maggots feed hidden inside the fruit. An infested pepper often turns red too early and starts to rot from the inside, with the grub tucked away where you cannot see it. Slim, thin-walled peppers like cayenne are much less bothered than fat-walled bell peppers.
seasoned: Adult flies puncture young pods to lay eggs, and the cream-colored larvae tunnel and feed inside the fruit for about 18 days; maggot-damaged peppers often color up (turn red) prematurely and begin to rot from within, with the larva hidden inside. Thin-walled, slender types such as cayenne are noted to suffer far less than thick-walled bell and pimento peppers, so cayenne is a relatively low-susceptibility host.

beginner: The maggot of a small fly that lays its eggs in young peppers in summer. It mostly attacks thick-walled peppers, so slim cayenne is much less at risk, though not completely safe where the fly is around.
seasoned: The pepper maggot, the larva of a small fly that lays eggs in developing pods in mid to late summer. It is most damaging on thick-walled peppers; cayenne and other slender, thin-walled, hot types are documented as far less affected, though not immune where the fly is active.

beginner: You cannot save an infested pepper, so pick off and throw away any that rot or color up early, and put fallen fruit in the trash, not the compost. Cayenne is rarely hit hard, so cleaning up damaged fruit is usually all a home garden needs.
seasoned: There is no rescue for an infested pod: remove and destroy affected fruit promptly, and drop fallen and culled peppers into the trash rather than the compost so larvae do not complete development in the garden. Where the fly is a known local problem, a well-timed labeled insecticide at first fly activity is the reliable control, but on cayenne the low susceptibility usually makes sanitation enough.

beginner: Cayenne's slim, thin walls already make it a poor target, so the main thing is to clean up any dropped or damaged peppers during the season and move peppers to a new spot each year. Where the fly is a known local pest, covering plants helps.
seasoned: Grow the thin-walled hot types (cayenne among them) that the maggot largely avoids, clean up dropped and cull fruit through the season, and rotate away from where peppers grew. In areas with a known pepper-maggot history, cover plants or time a labeled spray to first adult activity.

beginner: A small weevil whose grubs feed inside the buds and pods. Affected buds and flowers turn yellow and drop, pods may fall early or come out misshapen, and inside an infested pepper looks dark and full of grub droppings. It is mostly a warm-South problem and does not survive cold winters.
seasoned: Adults feed on foliage, buds, and tender pods, but the larvae do the real harm: infested buds and blossoms yellow and drop, pods may drop prematurely or grow misshapen, and the inside of an affected pod turns dark and fills with frass. It is chiefly a problem in the warm South (Florida, the Gulf, the Southwest) where the weevil can persist; it cannot overwinter in colder regions.

beginner: A tiny weevil whose grubs grow up inside pepper buds and pods. It is a warm-climate pest, common in Florida and the Gulf, and often arrives on infested plants. It cannot survive cold winters, so northern gardens rarely see it.
seasoned: The pepper weevil, a small snout beetle whose larvae develop inside buds and pods. It is a serious pepper pest in Florida, the Gulf Coast, and the warm Southwest, moving in on infested transplants or from nearby solanaceous weeds and abandoned pepper plantings; in cold-winter regions it does not establish.

beginner: You cannot save an infested pepper, so gather up and throw away any dropped buds and pods (in the trash, not the compost) to slow it down, and pull nearby weedy nightshades. In warm areas where it is common, you may need a labeled spray, and always start with healthy, locally grown plants.
seasoned: There is no home-garden cure for an infested pod. Pick up and destroy dropped buds and pods promptly (in the trash, not the compost) to break the cycle, remove volunteer peppers and solanaceous weeds that harbor the weevil, and in endemic areas a labeled insecticide program is often needed for a clean crop. Start with clean, locally grown transplants.

beginner: Start with healthy transplants grown in your area, not shipped in from warm regions where the weevil lives, clean up dropped peppers during the season, pull weedy nightshades, and clear out old plants at season's end. Keeping the garden clean is the main defense.
seasoned: Buy transplants grown where the pepper weevil is not established rather than importing the problem, clean up dropped fruit and nightshade weeds through the season, and remove and destroy spent plantings promptly so the weevil has nowhere to carry over. Rotation and garden sanitation are the backbone of control.

beginner: Whole leaves vanish overnight, leaving just the veins, sometimes with gouged pods, and dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight. Peppers are a side dish for it compared with tomato, but even a few can strip a plant.
seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots or the surface of a pod, are stripped or gouged overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to three or four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass. Peppers are a secondary host, so damage is usually less than on tomato, but a few caterpillars can defoliate a plant fast.

beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on pepper and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage, though they prefer tomatoes.
seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including pepper from midsummer on. Given their size, even a few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage, though peppers are less preferred than tomato.

beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.

beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.
seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.

beginner: A young pepper plant is found toppled, cut right through at the soil line, as if snipped. It happens overnight, soon after planting. Sometimes the same caterpillars climb up and chew leaves and fruit too.
seasoned: Young transplants are found cut off cleanly at or just above the soil line, felled overnight, with the severed plant lying nearby. Climbing cutworms may also feed on leaves and fruit higher up. The damage strikes right after transplanting, when the loss of a stem at the base kills the whole young plant.

beginner: Fat caterpillars that hide in the soil during the day and chew through young stems at night. They are worst on new transplants in spring, especially in ground that was recently grass or weeds.
seasoned: Cutworms, the soil-dwelling larvae of several moths, that shelter in the soil by day and sever young stems at night. They are worst on newly set transplants in spring, especially in beds recently turned from sod or weeds.

beginner: Put a collar around each young plant, such as a cardboard tube or a cup with the bottom cut out, pushed a little into the soil, so cutworms cannot reach the stem. If a plant is cut down, dig in the soil nearby to find and remove the curled caterpillar.
seasoned: Set a collar (a cardboard tube, tin can, or cup with the bottom removed) around each transplant, pushed an inch into the soil, to block cutworms. Check for and hand-pick the curled gray caterpillars in the soil around a felled plant at dusk, and keep beds clear of the weeds and debris they shelter in.

beginner: Put a protective collar around each plant when you set it out, clear weeds and debris from the bed ahead of time, and turn the soil before planting to expose the caterpillars. Beds that were recently lawn are the riskiest.
seasoned: Ring transplants with collars at planting, clear the bed of weeds and old plant debris a couple of weeks ahead, and lightly cultivate the soil before planting to expose and disrupt overwintering larvae. Beds newly broken from lawn are highest-risk.

beginner: Small wet-looking spots on the leaves turn brown with a yellow ring, and badly spotted leaves drop off, which lets the sun scald the exposed peppers. The fruit can develop dark, raised, scabby spots. It is worst in warm, rainy weather.
seasoned: Small, water-soaked spots on the leaves enlarge and turn dark brown with a yellow halo, and heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop prematurely; the resulting defoliation exposes the pods to sunscald. On the fruit, small raised blisters develop into dark brown, scabby, cracked lesions. It is one of the most damaging pepper diseases in warm, wet weather.

beginner: A bacterial disease carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in splashing water and on wet hands and tools. It loves warm, wet weather. Starting with clean seed and keeping leaves dry are the main defenses.
seasoned: Xanthomonas bacteria that are seed- and debris-borne and spread in splashing water and on hands and tools, thriving in warm, humid, rainy conditions. Once established in wet weather it moves fast, so clean seed, resistant varieties, and dry foliage are the keys to control.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so remove the worst-affected leaves and plants and stay out of the patch when it is wet. A copper spray can slow it down in rainy spells but will not cure it. Keeping the leaves dry matters most.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove badly affected leaves and plants and avoid working among wet plants. Copper-based sprays can slow spread as a protectant in wet spells but do not cure the disease. Focus on limiting splash and moisture.

beginner: Use clean, resistant seed and healthy transplants, do not plant peppers in the same spot for several years, water at the soil instead of over the leaves, mulch, and clean up old plants at the end of the season. Do not work among the plants while they are wet.
seasoned: Start with certified disease-free or resistant seed and transplants, rotate peppers out of the bed for several years, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, avoid handling wet plants, and remove crop debris at season's end.

beginner: The leaves turn a patchy light-and-dark green, get distorted or crinkled, and the plant is stunted, with mottled or oddly ripening peppers. Several viruses cause this, usually spread by aphids, and none can be cured. Tobacco products can carry one of these viruses to peppers on your hands.
seasoned: Leaves become mottled light and dark green, distorted, sometimes crinkled or narrowed, and the plant stunts; fruit may be mottled, distorted, or ripen unevenly. Several viruses cause this picture (tobacco and cucumber mosaic, pepper mottle, potato virus Y, and others), often spread by aphids, and there is no cure. Tobacco mosaic can also be carried on hands after handling tobacco.

beginner: A group of viruses spread mainly by aphids, and one of them by tobacco on your hands. There is no cure, so the whole game is prevention: keep aphids down and pull out infected plants before they spread it.
seasoned: A complex of viruses (tobacco mosaic, cucumber mosaic, pepper mottle, potato virus Y, and others) transmitted chiefly by aphids probing plant to plant, and in the case of tobacco mosaic by contaminated hands and tools. Because there is no cure, control is entirely about prevention: manage aphids and remove infected plants.

beginner: There is no cure. Pull out and destroy infected plants so they do not spread it to the rest. Keep aphids under control, and wash your hands after handling tobacco before touching your peppers. Do not compost sick plants.
seasoned: There is no treatment; promptly remove and destroy infected plants to limit spread to healthy ones. Control the aphids that vector the viruses, and wash hands after any tobacco use before touching peppers. Do not compost infected plants.

beginner: Look for resistant varieties, start with healthy plants, keep aphids down, remove infected plants right away, control weeds, and do not handle peppers right after using tobacco. Prevention is the only tool with viruses.
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties where available, start with clean transplants, control aphids early with the measures above, use reflective mulch to repel them from young plants, remove infected plants at first sign, keep weeds that host viruses down, and avoid tobacco contact with the crop.

beginner: Dark, wet-looking patches form on the stem near the soil, girdle it, and the whole plant wilts and dies quickly, often after heavy rain or in a soggy spot. It can also rot the fruit with white fuzzy growth. It lives in the soil for years and spreads fast in warm, wet ground.
seasoned: Dark, water-soaked lesions develop on the crown and stem at or near the soil line, turn brown, and girdle the stem, so the whole plant wilts and dies suddenly, often after heavy rain or in a poorly drained spot. The disease can also cause dark leaf lesions and a firm fruit rot with white, cottony mold. It persists in soil for years and spreads fast in warm, wet, saturated conditions.

beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing and running water, attacking plants in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts, so good drainage is the main way to keep it out.
seasoned: Phytophthora capsici, a water mold that thrives in saturated soil and spreads in splashing and running water. It survives in soil and debris and moves rapidly in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground and in low spots that stay wet, which is why drainage is the central control.

beginner: There is no home cure once plants collapse. Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage right away. Prevention is really the only tool.
seasoned: There is no home-garden cure once plants collapse; remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly and improve drainage immediately. Because the pathogen persists in soil, control is preventive and drainage-based rather than curative.

beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away, avoid soggy low spots, water at the soil, do not overwater, and rotate away from peppers, tomatoes, and squash. Good drainage is the whole game with this one.
seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds, avoid low spots that stay wet, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, do not overwater, rotate away from peppers and other solanaceous and cucurbit crops on a long cycle, and keep pods up off saturated soil.

beginner: Small, sunken, round spots form on the peppers, sometimes in rings, with a pink or salmon ooze in the middle. It usually shows up as the fruit ripens, so peppers left to turn fully red are most at risk in warm, wet weather. It can spot leaves and stems too.
seasoned: Small, sunken, circular lesions appear on the pods, often in concentric rings, and develop moist masses of salmon-to-pink spores in the center. It typically shows up as the fruit ripens (a ripe-fruit rot), and because infection can be latent, cayenne left to color fully red for drying is especially exposed in warm, wet seasons. It also spots leaves and stems.

beginner: A fungus carried on seed and old debris that spreads in splashing water and loves warm, wet weather. It often infects green fruit quietly and then shows up as the peppers ripen, so red-ripe cayenne is most at risk.
seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi that are seed- and debris-borne and spread in splashing water, favored by warm, humid, wet weather. Infections often stay latent in green fruit and break out as the pods ripen, which matters for cayenne grown for red, dried pods.

beginner: Pick off and throw away infected peppers right away, and keep the plants and fruit as dry as you can. A labeled fungicide can protect the rest in a wet spell but cannot cure a rotting pod. In wet weather, pick ripe peppers promptly instead of leaving them on the plant.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected pods promptly to reduce spore load, and keep foliage and fruit as dry as possible. Copper or other labeled fungicides can protect healthy fruit in a wet season but will not cure infected pods. Harvest ripening pods promptly rather than leaving them out in wet weather.

beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, rotate your peppers, water at the soil, mulch, give plants room for airflow, and pick ripe peppers promptly in wet weather rather than leaving them to sit and rot.
seasoned: Start with clean or treated seed and disease-free transplants, rotate peppers on a long cycle, water at the soil, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, remove crop debris, and pick pods as they ripen rather than holding fully ripe fruit on the plant through wet spells.

beginner: A tan, sunken, leathery spot appears on the bottom end of the pepper. It is not a disease you can catch or spray: it comes from the fruit not getting enough calcium, which happens when watering is uneven, not usually because the soil lacks calcium. The first peppers of the season are the usual victims.
seasoned: A tan, sunken, leathery patch forms at the blossom end of the pod (the end away from the stem), sometimes mistaken for sunscald. It is not caused by a pathogen: it is a physiological disorder from a local calcium shortage in the fruit, driven by uneven soil moisture rather than by low soil calcium, since calcium moves to the fruit only with a steady water supply. The first pods of the season are most often affected.

beginner: The developing pepper cannot get enough calcium to its far end, which happens when the soil dries out and then gets flooded. It is almost always an uneven-watering problem, not a lack of calcium in your soil.
seasoned: A calcium-transport problem within the plant: calcium is carried to the developing pod in the water stream, so when the soil swings from dry to wet the fruit is starved of calcium at its far end even if the soil has plenty. Uneven watering, drought stress, and root damage are the real triggers, not a soil calcium deficit in most gardens.

beginner: You cannot fix a pepper that already has it, so pick off affected pods and focus on steady watering going forward. Mulch and water regularly and deeply, and the later peppers should come in clean. Calcium sprays usually do not help, since the real issue is uneven watering.
seasoned: There is no cure for an affected pod; the fix is cultural and forward-looking. Even out soil moisture with mulch and regular deep watering, remove affected pods so the plant redirects energy, and expect later fruit to come in clean once watering is steady. Calcium sprays are largely ineffective because the problem is water-driven transport, not soil calcium.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and never let it go bone-dry and then flood it. Mulch to hold moisture, water deeply and regularly, especially in hot weather, and go easy on nitrogen. Steady watering prevents almost all of it.
seasoned: Keep the soil uniformly moist, never letting it dry out between waterings, mulch to buffer moisture, water deeply and regularly especially in heat, avoid heavy nitrogen and root disturbance that stress uptake, and make sure the bed drains so roots stay healthy. Steady moisture is the whole prevention.

beginner: Give cayenne about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day. Keeping the water steady matters a lot, since letting the soil dry out and then flooding it causes blossom-end rot on the peppers. Plants in pots dry out much faster and may need checking daily in summer.
seasoned: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. As a warm-season crop grown through the hottest part of the year, cayenne transpires heavily in summer, and container plants dry out far faster still. The wider Solanaceae, tomato, potato, and eggplant, share that complex, so rotate them as a group and avoid following any of them. Clear and remove spent plants and dropped fruit at season's end rather than tilling them in.

beginner: Cayenne is a hot pepper, a warm-season plant in the same family as tomatoes and grown for its long, slim, fiery-hot pods. The peppers are thin and tapering, about 4 to 6 inches, often a little curved and wrinkled, and they ripen from green to bright red. They are seriously hot, roughly 25,000 to 50,000 on the Scoville heat scale, several times hotter than a jalapeno. The classic use is drying: you let the pods turn fully red, then string them up to dry or use a dehydrator and grind them into cayenne powder to keep all year. You grow cayenne much like a tomato, from a transplant set into warm soil after the last frost, with a few pepper quirks: the seeds are slow and like real warmth, the plant sulks if set out into cold soil, you feed it lightly (too much nitrogen gives all leaves and few peppers), and in very hot weather it drops its flowers and stops setting for a while, picking back up as it cools. The plant is compact and does not need staking, and one plant makes a lot of pods over a long season. Watch for aphids, flea beetles on young plants, and a few diseases, and keep the water steady to avoid blossom-end rot. seasoned: Cayenne is a hot pepper (Capsicum annuum), a warm-season fruiting vegetable in the nightshade family grown for its long, slender, fiery pods. The fruit is the signature: thin-walled, tapering, and typically 4 to 6 inches, often curved and wrinkled, ripening from waxy green to bright red, and rating roughly 25,000 to 50,000 Scoville heat units, several times hotter than a jalapeno (about 2,500 to 8,000). Classically it is grown for drying: the pods are left to color fully red, then strung and hung or run through a dehydrator and ground into cayenne powder, a summer's heat put by for the year. Culturally it is a tomato relative and grown much the same way, a self-fertile transplant crop set into warm soil after frost, but with a few pepper particulars: it germinates slowly and wants real warmth, sulks if planted cold, is a moderate feeder that runs to leaf if over-fed with nitrogen, and, like tomato, drops its blossoms and pauses fruit set in extreme heat (days above about 90°F, nights above 75°F), so in the hot deserts and deep South the crop pauses through the peak of summer and flushes again in fall. The plant is compact and self-supporting, needs no staking, and is prolific over a long season. Its pests are aphids (and the viruses they carry), flea beetles on seedlings, and the pepper maggot and pepper weevil of warmer regions, to which the thin-walled cayenne is relatively less prone; its diseases are bacterial leaf spot, the mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, and the ripe-fruit rot of anthracnose, plus the physiological blossom-end rot that steady watering prevents. Handle the pods with gloves: the capsaicin that makes them hot is an oil that burns skin and eyes.
